TITLE: How to Build an AI Workstation in 2026: Parts, Budgets and Configurations for Local LLMs and Training
LABEL: BUYING GUIDE
IMG: How to Build an AI Workstation
EXCERPT: A complete guide to building a PC for AI: choosing the GPU, CPU, RAM, storage, motherboard, power supply and cooling for local LLMs, Stable Diffusion and fine-tuning, with four example builds from entry level to multi-GPU, plus Mac and DGX Spark alternatives and common mistakes.
KEY: An AI workstation is built around the GPU: its VRAM decides which models you can run and its memory bandwidth decides how fast. Then make sure the rest of the system does not hold it back: system RAM at least equal to, ideally double, your total VRAM; a fast NVMe SSD with plenty of space for model files; a CPU and motherboard with enough PCIe lanes for your GPUs; and a high-quality power supply with headroom (1,000 W or more for an RTX 5090). Typical builds range from a 16 GB entry rig for 7B–14B models to multi-GPU or 96 GB workstation-card setups for 70B models and serious fine-tuning.
content:
Short answer

An AI workstation is built around the GPU: its VRAM decides which models you can run and its memory bandwidth decides how fast. Then make sure the rest of the system does not hold it back: system RAM at least equal to, ideally double, your total VRAM; a fast NVMe SSD with plenty of space for model files; a CPU and motherboard with enough PCIe lanes for your GPUs; and a high-quality power supply with headroom (1,000 W or more for an RTX 5090). Typical builds range from a 16 GB entry rig for 7B–14B models to multi-GPU or 96 GB workstation-card setups for 70B models and serious fine-tuning.

Step 1: Decide what you will run

Use our VRAM guide, the VRAM calculator and best GPU for local LLMs to size your needs. If you mainly generate images, see best GPU for Stable Diffusion; for training, see best GPU for deep learning.

Step 2: Choose the GPU

Compare the top two consumer options in RTX 5090 vs RTX 4090 for AI. NVIDIA remains the easiest choice because almost every AI tool supports CUDA; see AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.

Step 3: CPU and motherboard

The CPU matters less than the GPU for AI, but it handles data loading, tokenization, and running models that spill out of VRAM.

  • Single GPU: a modern 8–16 core desktop CPU (AMD Ryzen 7/9 or Intel Core Ultra 7/9) is plenty.
  • Two GPUs: check that the motherboard can run both slots at x8 PCIe or better, with enough physical space between cards.
  • Three or more GPUs: a workstation platform such as AMD Threadripper or Intel Xeon W provides many more PCIe lanes and memory channels.
  • CPU offloading: if you plan to run models larger than your VRAM using system RAM (for example large MoE models in llama.cpp), more memory channels and bandwidth help a lot.

Step 4: System RAM

Rule of thumb: at least as much RAM as total VRAM, ideally double, so models can be loaded, converted and partly offloaded without swapping. DRAM prices rose sharply in 2026, so plan your budget accordingly; see why GPU prices are rising.

Step 5: Storage

  • Primary: a PCIe 4.0 or 5.0 NVMe SSD of 2 TB or more. Model files are large: a single 70B model at Q4 is about 40 GB, and collections grow fast.
  • Secondary: additional NVMe or SATA SSDs for datasets and checkpoints.
  • Backups: an external drive or NAS for important fine-tuned models and data.

Fast storage shortens model loading times and keeps training pipelines fed.

Step 6: Power supply

Choose an ATX 3.1 power supply from a reputable brand with the native 12V-2x6 connector for modern NVIDIA cards, and seat the connector fully. AI workloads can run at full power for hours, so quality and headroom matter more than for gaming.

Step 7: Cooling and case

  • Choose a large case with strong front-to-back airflow and space for long GPUs.
  • For two or more GPUs, prefer blower-style or well-spaced cards, or open-frame designs.
  • Keep the room ventilated; a 600 W GPU running for hours produces a lot of heat.
  • Consider undervolting or setting a power limit (for example 80–90% of maximum): AI throughput often drops only slightly while temperatures and noise fall substantially.

Four example builds

Exact prices change frequently, especially for GPUs and memory, so check current listings when you buy.

Alternatives to building a PC

Software setup checklist

1. Install the latest NVIDIA driver (and the CUDA toolkit if you develop GPU code; see What is CUDA?). 2. On Linux or Windows WSL2, install Python and a package manager such as uv or conda. 3. For chat with local models, install Ollama or LM Studio; see how to run an LLM locally. 4. For image generation, install ComfyUI or Forge. 5. For development and serving, install PyTorch, then vLLM or llama.cpp; see LLM inference engines compared. 6. Monitor temperatures and utilisation with nvidia-smi or nvtop.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Prioritising CPU over GPU: for AI, VRAM and bandwidth dominate.
  • Buying 8 GB GPUs: too little for modern models.
  • Too little system RAM: causes slow loading and failures when offloading.
  • Undersized power supplies: cause crashes under sustained AI load.
  • Ignoring physical space for multiple GPUs: large cards may not fit side by side.
  • Expecting NVLink on consumer cards: RTX 40 and 50 series cards do not support it.

Frequently asked questions

How much does an AI workstation cost?

From roughly the price of a mid-range gaming PC for an entry 16 GB build, to well over $10,000 for workstation cards or multi-GPU systems. GPU and memory prices fluctuate, so compare current listings.

Is one big GPU better than two smaller ones?

Usually yes. One GPU with more VRAM avoids the overhead of splitting models over PCIe. Two GPUs make sense when you need more total memory than any single affordable card offers.

Can I use a gaming PC for AI?

Yes. A gaming PC with an NVIDIA GPU of 12 GB or more is a good starting point. Upgrade RAM and storage if needed.

Linux or Windows for AI?

Linux has the best support for AI frameworks and servers. Windows works well for local tools like Ollama, LM Studio and ComfyUI, and WSL2 provides a Linux environment on Windows.

  • Ollama
  • llama.cpp on GitHub
  • ComfyUI on GitHub
  • TensorCore.si, GPU cloud price tracker

TITLE: Best GPU for Deep Learning and AI Training in 2026: From Students to Data Centers
LABEL: BUYING GUIDE
EXCERPT: Which GPU should you use to train neural networks in 2026? A practical guide for students, researchers, startups and enterprises: how much VRAM training really needs, the best consumer, workstation and data center GPUs, multi-GPU setups, AMD and Apple options, and when renting in the cloud beats buying.
KEY: The best GPU for deep learning training is the one that fits your model in memory with room for gradients and optimizer states. In 2026: students and hobbyists are best served by an RTX 5070 Ti/5080 (16 GB) or a used RTX 3090 (24 GB); serious individual researchers by the RTX 5090 (32 GB); labs and startups by the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB) or rented H100/H200; and large-scale training by H200, B200 or GB200 clusters in the cloud. Training needs roughly 4–8× more memory than running the same model, so VRAM matters even more than for inference.
content:
Short answer

The best GPU for deep learning training is the one that fits your model in memory with room for gradients and optimizer states. In 2026: students and hobbyists are best served by an RTX 5070 Ti/5080 (16 GB) or a used RTX 3090 (24 GB); serious individual researchers by the RTX 5090 (32 GB); labs and startups by the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB) or rented H100/H200; and large-scale training by H200, B200 or GB200 clusters in the cloud. Training needs roughly 4–8× more memory than running the same model, so VRAM matters even more than for inference.

Training vs inference: why requirements differ

Running a model (inference) needs memory for the weights. Training needs the weights plus gradients, optimizer states and activations. With mixed precision and the Adam optimizer, that is about 16 bytes per parameter before activations, versus 2 bytes per parameter to run in FP16. See AI training vs inference and mixed precision training.

Estimate your own case with the VRAM guide and fine-tuning guide.

What matters in a training GPU

1. VRAM capacity: decides model size, batch size and sequence length. 2. Tensor core throughput (BF16/FP8): decides how fast each step runs. See how tensor cores actually work. 3. Memory bandwidth: feeds the tensor cores; important for large models and attention. See GPU memory bandwidth. 4. Multi-GPU interconnect: NVLink is available on data center GPUs, not on GeForce cards. See NVLink and NVSwitch. 5. Software support: CUDA support is the most mature; AMD ROCm is improving. 6. Reliability features: ECC memory and validated drivers on workstation and data center cards.

Best GPUs by user type

Students and beginners

Independent researchers and developers

See RTX 5090 vs RTX 4090 for AI and is the RTX 5090 good for AI?.

Labs, startups and professionals

Large-scale training (usually rented)

Comparisons: H100 vs A100, H100 vs H200, B200 vs H100, B200 vs B300.

Should you buy or rent?

Today's on-demand prices from our GPU cloud price tracker (November 25, 2026): median about $2.19/hour for an A100, $3.92/hour for an H100, $4.95/hour for an H200 and $7.84/hour for a B200, with the cheapest providers well below the median. See rent vs buy a GPU and cloud GPU providers compared.

Quick cost estimate: a fine-tuning run needing 100 H100-hours costs roughly $180–$400 at current rates, far less than buying an H100.

Multi-GPU training tips

  • Data parallelism (each GPU trains on different batches) works fine over PCIe for many models.
  • Model parallelism for big models needs fast links; consumer GPUs lack NVLink, so use FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO to shard memory. See distributed training and parallelism.
  • Make sure your motherboard provides enough PCIe lanes, your power supply can handle the combined load, and cooling is adequate.

AMD, Apple and other options

  • AMD Instinct accelerators offer large memory and competitive performance in the cloud with ROCm; consumer Radeon cards are usable for some training but less supported. See AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.
  • Apple Silicon Macs are good for prototyping and fine-tuning small models with MLX, thanks to unified memory, but much slower than NVIDIA GPUs for serious training.
  • Google TPUs are excellent for large training jobs in Google Cloud with JAX. See TPU vs GPU.

Common mistakes

  • Buying for gaming benchmarks: training cares about VRAM and tensor performance, not frame rates.
  • Choosing 8 GB cards: too small for modern deep learning.
  • Ignoring power and cooling: high-end cards need large power supplies and good airflow.
  • Over-buying: many people would spend less renting H100s for occasional big runs.
  • Forgetting the rest of the system: slow storage or too little RAM can starve the GPU. See how to build an AI workstation.

Frequently asked questions

What is the minimum GPU for deep learning?

A GPU with at least 8 GB of VRAM can handle introductory courses, but 12–16 GB is a much better minimum in 2026, especially for working with transformers.

Is the RTX 5090 good enough for training LLMs?

It is excellent for fine-tuning and training small to mid-sized models. Pre-training large LLMs requires many data center GPUs.

Is the H100 still worth renting in 2026?

Yes. It remains widely available, well supported and often the best price-performance option for many training jobs, though H200 and B200 are faster for large models.

Do I need ECC memory for deep learning?

Not for learning and experiments. For long, expensive training runs in production, ECC on workstation and data center GPUs reduces the risk of silent errors.

content:
Short answer

Cloud GPU providers fall into three groups. Hyperscalers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle) cost the most per GPU-hour but offer the deepest ecosystems and enterprise compliance. Specialist GPU clouds (such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Crusoe, Together AI, Hyperstack) focus on AI with lower prices and strong multi-node clusters. Marketplaces and serverless platforms (such as RunPod, Vast.ai, Modal, Beam) are the cheapest and quickest to start for individuals and inference. Based on our daily tracker on November 25, 2026, the median H100 price is about $3.92/hour, ranging from $1.80 to over $11 depending on provider. Price is only part of the decision: networking, availability, storage and support matter as much for real projects.

The three types of GPU cloud

*Single-GPU on-demand prices from our tracker on November 25, 2026; multi-GPU instances are divided by GPU count. Prices change frequently, so check the live GPU cloud price tracker.

Today's prices at a glance

Source: TensorCore.si daily tracker, November 25, 2026. Detailed per-GPU guides: H100 price, H200 price, B200 price and cheapest cloud GPU.

Hyperscalers: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle

Strengths:

  • Huge global footprint, mature security and compliance certifications.
  • Deep integration with storage, databases, networking, identity and managed AI services.
  • Large reserved and committed-use discounts for enterprises.
  • Proprietary accelerators too: Google TPUs, AWS Trainium and Inferentia.

Weaknesses:

  • The highest on-demand GPU prices in our tracker, often two to three times specialist clouds.
  • GPU quotas may require approval; the newest GPUs often come in large instance sizes.
  • Data egress fees can be significant when moving datasets or models out.

Choose a hyperscaler if: your organisation already runs there, needs specific compliance, or wants TPUs or Trainium. See AWS vs Google Cloud vs Azure GPU pricing.

Specialist GPU clouds

Strengths:

  • Built specifically for AI: modern NVIDIA GPUs, high-speed InfiniBand or AI Ethernet for multi-node training, and Kubernetes or Slurm support.
  • Lower prices than hyperscalers, often with simple per-hour billing and little or no egress cost.
  • Early access to new GPUs like B200 and GB200 in some cases.

Weaknesses:

  • Narrower catalogues of non-GPU services.
  • Popular GPUs can sell out; large clusters often require reservations.
  • Support levels and enterprise features vary between providers.

Choose a specialist cloud if: you are training or fine-tuning models, need multi-node clusters, or want the best price-performance for serious AI work.

Marketplaces and serverless GPU platforms

Strengths:

  • Lowest prices, especially for consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090 and 5090 (from roughly $0.26–$0.29 per hour in our tracker).
  • Start in minutes with templates for Jupyter, ComfyUI, vLLM and more.
  • Serverless platforms bill by the second and scale to zero for inference APIs.

Weaknesses:

  • Community-hosted machines vary in reliability, security and network speed.
  • Usually single-node; limited fast interconnect for distributed training.
  • Data privacy depends on the host; read terms carefully for sensitive data.

Choose a marketplace if: you are learning, experimenting, running Stable Diffusion or small LLMs, or deploying bursty inference.

What to compare beyond price

SXM vs PCIe: a common pricing trap

Many cheaper listings are PCIe versions of the H100, which have lower power limits, lower memory bandwidth (about 2.0 TB/s versus 3.35 TB/s for SXM) and no NVLink between GPUs. For multi-GPU training and fast inference, SXM systems (often sold as 8-GPU HGX servers) are usually worth the higher price. Always check the exact configuration. See how to read a GPU spec sheet.

On-demand vs spot vs reserved

Which provider type fits your use case?

A checklist before you rent

1. Estimate GPU memory needed; see how much VRAM for an LLM. 2. Decide single GPU vs multi-GPU vs multi-node. 3. Compare current prices on the GPU cloud price tracker. 4. Confirm SXM vs PCIe and the interconnect. 5. Check storage, egress and billing granularity. 6. Test with a small job before committing. 7. Set budget alerts and shut down idle instances. 8. For long jobs, checkpoint frequently.

Weighing renting against owning hardware? Read rent vs buy a GPU and best GPU for deep learning.

Frequently asked questions

Which cloud has the cheapest H100?

It changes daily. On November 25, 2026, the lowest on-demand H100 price in our tracker was about $1.80 per hour. Check the live tracker for today's cheapest providers.

Why are AWS, Google Cloud and Azure more expensive?

Hyperscaler prices include extensive infrastructure, compliance, support and integrated services, and their headline on-demand rates assume most large customers negotiate discounts or reserve capacity.

Are marketplace GPUs safe for private data?

It depends on the host. Many marketplaces offer secure or data-center-grade tiers. For sensitive data, use providers with clear security certifications and isolation.

Is it cheaper to rent or buy a GPU?

For occasional or large-scale workloads, renting is usually cheaper. For constant, long-term use of a single GPU, buying can pay off. See rent vs buy a GPU.

TITLE: How Tensor Cores Work: MMA Instructions, Tiles and Data Flow From Volta to Blackwell
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: A deep technical look inside NVIDIA tensor cores: the matrix multiply-accumulate operation, tile shapes, how warps feed tensor cores, MMA, wgmma and tcgen05 instructions, Tensor Memory, data movement with TMA, sparsity and precision, and why tensor cores are so much faster than CUDA cores.
KEY: To understand how tensor cores work, start with what they are: a tensor core is a hardware unit that computes a small matrix multiply-accumulate, D = A × B + C, in one operation, instead of thousands of individual multiplications. Groups of GPU threads cooperatively load tiles of matrices A and B, the tensor core multiplies them in low precision (FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4) and adds the result to a higher-precision accumulator. Each generation has made the tiles larger and the programming model more asynchronous: from warp-level MMA on Volta and Ampere, to warpgroup-level wgmma with the Tensor Memory Accelerator on Hopper, to tcgen05 instructions with dedicated Tensor Memory on data center Blackwell. That evolution is why tensor cores deliver most of a modern GPU's AI performance.
content:
Short answer

To understand how tensor cores work, start with what they are: a tensor core is a hardware unit that computes a small matrix multiply-accumulate, D = A × B + C, in one operation, instead of thousands of individual multiplications. Groups of GPU threads cooperatively load tiles of matrices A and B, the tensor core multiplies them in low precision (FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4) and adds the result to a higher-precision accumulator. Each generation has made the tiles larger and the programming model more asynchronous: from warp-level MMA on Volta and Ampere, to warpgroup-level wgmma with the Tensor Memory Accelerator on Hopper, to tcgen05 instructions with dedicated Tensor Memory on data center Blackwell. That evolution is why tensor cores deliver most of a modern GPU's AI performance.

The one operation that runs AI

Nearly every layer in a neural network is a matrix multiplication: inputs times weights. A transformer's attention and feed-forward layers, a convolution in an image model, an embedding projection: all reduce to multiplying large matrices. If you can multiply matrices faster, you make AI faster. For the basics, start with What is a tensor core?.

A regular GPU core (a CUDA core) performs one fused multiply-add on two numbers per clock. A tensor core performs an entire small matrix multiply-accumulate per clock or a few clocks, sharing data between many multipliers so that each value loaded from memory is reused many times.

The math: matrix multiply-accumulate

D = A × B + C

A: M × K matrix   (low precision, e.g. FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4)
B: K × N matrix   (low precision)
C, D: M × N matrix (accumulator, usually FP32 or FP16)

Every output element of D is a dot product of a row of A and a column of B, plus the matching element of C. For a 16 × 8 × 16 tile, that is 16 × 8 × 16 = 2,048 multiply-adds done as one instruction.

Two design choices make this efficient:

1. Data reuse: each element of A is used N times and each element of B is used M times. Larger tiles mean more arithmetic per byte loaded, which matters because memory is slower than math. See GPU memory bandwidth and the roofline model. 2. Mixed precision: inputs in small formats (fewer bits, more operations per watt), accumulation in FP32 (to avoid rounding errors piling up over long dot products). See FP16 vs BF16 vs FP8 vs FP4 and mixed precision training.

How a GPU feeds its tensor cores

A GPU is made of streaming multiprocessors (SMs). Each SM contains several tensor cores alongside CUDA cores, registers and shared memory. The data path for a large matrix multiply looks like this:

1. Global memory (HBM or GDDR): the full matrices live here. 2. Shared memory / L1: each thread block copies tiles of A and B into fast on-chip memory. 3. Registers or Tensor Memory: smaller fragments are staged for the tensor core. 4. Tensor core: performs the MMA on the fragments, accumulating results. 5. Write back: finished tiles of D are written to global memory.

High-performance kernels pipeline these steps so data for the next tile is loading while the current tile is being multiplied. Explore the hardware basics in how a GPU works.

The generational evolution

For the full lineage, see tensor core generations and Hopper vs Blackwell.

Volta to Ampere: warp-level MMA

On Volta, Turing and Ampere, a warp of 32 threads executes a matrix instruction together. Each thread holds a few elements of the A, B and C fragments in its registers, and the hardware assembles them into the full tile. In CUDA C++ this is exposed through the wmma API or the lower-level PTX mma.sync instruction, for example with shapes like m16n8k16.

Ampere added asynchronous copies (cp.async), letting threads start copying the next tile from global to shared memory without waiting, and 2:4 structured sparsity, where tensor cores skip zeroed weights for up to twice the throughput. See structured sparsity explained.

Limitation: the warp had to wait for each mma.sync to finish, and registers had to hold both inputs and accumulators, limiting tile sizes.

Hopper: warpgroups, wgmma and TMA

Hopper's H100 introduced three big changes:

  • wgmma (warpgroup MMA): four warps (128 threads) issue one large, asynchronous matrix instruction. Operands can come directly from shared memory, so threads don't have to load everything into registers first. Threads can keep doing other work while the tensor cores compute.
  • Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA): a dedicated engine that copies multi-dimensional tiles between global and shared memory with a single instruction, freeing threads from address calculations.
  • Thread block clusters and distributed shared memory: groups of SMs can share data in each other's shared memory.

Combined with FP8 support and the Transformer Engine, which manages scaling factors for FP8, these features let H100 kernels keep tensor cores much busier than earlier GPUs. Kernels like FlashAttention version 3 were written specifically to exploit wgmma and TMA.

Blackwell: tcgen05 and Tensor Memory

Data center Blackwell (B200, GB200) moves further toward a dedicated tensor engine:

  • tcgen05 instructions: a single thread can launch a large MMA on behalf of the whole block, rather than requiring a warpgroup to participate.
  • Tensor Memory (TMEM): a dedicated on-chip memory per SM for accumulators, so large results no longer consume general-purpose registers. Data is moved between TMEM and registers explicitly.
  • 2-CTA MMA: two SMs can cooperate on one larger matrix multiply, increasing data reuse.
  • FP4 and FP6 with block scaling: formats like NVFP4 attach a shared scale factor to small blocks of values, keeping accuracy while doubling throughput over FP8.

The result is much larger effective tiles and higher utilisation. Consumer Blackwell (RTX 50 series) adds FP4 support but keeps a warp-level MMA programming model rather than the data center tcgen05 path.

Why tensor cores are so much faster

On an H100 SXM, dense BF16 tensor throughput is about 989 TFLOPS, while standard FP32 CUDA core throughput is roughly 67 TFLOPS. That gap of more than 10× is why AI frameworks route matrix work to tensor cores whenever possible. See tensor cores vs CUDA cores.

When tensor cores sit idle

Peak TFLOPS are rarely achieved. Common reasons:

  • Memory-bound workloads: single-user LLM decoding reads every weight for each token, so the GPU waits on memory, not math. See prefill vs decode.
  • Awkward shapes: matrix dimensions that are not multiples of 8, 16 or 64 waste parts of each tile.
  • Non-matrix operations: softmax, normalisation and activations run on CUDA cores and can become bottlenecks.
  • Poor pipelining: if data movement is not overlapped with compute, tensor cores wait.

Real training typically reaches 35–50% of peak; see MFU explained.

How developers use tensor cores

A quick check that tensor cores are used in PyTorch: enable BF16 autocast and keep matrix dimensions multiples of 8 or 16. For a hands-on start with GPU programming, see write your first CUDA kernel.

import torch
a = torch.randn(8192, 8192, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
b = torch.randn(8192, 8192, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
c = a @ b   # dispatched to tensor cores via cuBLAS

Frequently asked questions

How many tensor cores does a GPU have?

It varies: an H100 SXM has 528 tensor cores (4 per SM across 132 SMs), and an RTX 5090 has 680. Raw counts are not comparable across generations because each newer tensor core does much more work per clock.

Do tensor cores only work for AI?

They accelerate any workload built on dense matrix multiplication, including some scientific computing (with FP64 tensor cores on data center GPUs), graphics features like DLSS, and signal processing.

Are AMD and Intel GPUs equipped with tensor cores?

They have equivalent units under different names: AMD Matrix Cores and WMMA units, Intel XMX engines. See tensor cores vs AMD Matrix Cores vs Intel XMX.

Why are new tensor cores focused on smaller number formats?

Fewer bits per number means more operations per clock, less memory traffic and less energy per operation. With careful scaling, FP8 and FP4 keep model quality close to higher precision for many workloads.

Sources and further reading

  • NVIDIA, CUDA C++ Programming Guide: Warp Matrix Functions
  • NVIDIA, Parallel Thread Execution (PTX) ISA
  • NVIDIA, NVIDIA Hopper Architecture In-Depth
  • NVIDIA, Blackwell architecture
  • NVIDIA, CUTLASS on GitHub
  • Shah et al., FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision (2024)

TITLE: RTX 5090 vs RTX 4090 for AI: Specs, LLM Speed, Stable Diffusion and Which to Buy
LABEL: COMPARISON
EXCERPT: Is the RTX 5090 worth it over the RTX 4090 for AI? A detailed comparison of specs, VRAM, memory bandwidth, tensor cores and FP4, what each runs for local LLMs and Stable Diffusion, power and cost, used-market value and cloud rental prices.
KEY: In the RTX 5090 vs RTX 4090 comparison for AI, the RTX 5090 beats the RTX 4090 in the two specs that matter most: 32 GB vs 24 GB of VRAM and about 1.8 TB/s vs 1.0 TB/s of memory bandwidth. That means it fits larger models (such as 32B LLMs at higher quality and full-precision FLUX) and generates tokens up to roughly 1.7× faster in memory-bound workloads, plus FP4 support on fifth-generation tensor cores. The 4090 remains a strong card, especially on the used market. Choose the 5090 if you need the extra 8 GB or maximum speed; choose a used 4090 (or even a 3090) if value matters more.
content:
Short answer

In the RTX 5090 vs RTX 4090 comparison for AI, the RTX 5090 beats the RTX 4090 in the two specs that matter most: 32 GB vs 24 GB of VRAM and about 1.8 TB/s vs 1.0 TB/s of memory bandwidth. That means it fits larger models (such as 32B LLMs at higher quality and full-precision FLUX) and generates tokens up to roughly 1.7× faster in memory-bound workloads, plus FP4 support on fifth-generation tensor cores. The 4090 remains a strong card, especially on the used market. Choose the 5090 if you need the extra 8 GB or maximum speed; choose a used 4090 (or even a 3090) if value matters more.

Specifications side by side

Note that NVIDIA's AI TOPS figures compare FP4 on the 5090 with FP8 on the 4090, and include sparsity, so they overstate the real-world difference. See TOPS vs TFLOPS and how to read a GPU spec sheet.

Why VRAM and bandwidth matter most

  • VRAM decides what fits. If a model does not fit, it must be quantized more aggressively or partly offloaded to system RAM, which is much slower. See What is VRAM?.
  • Bandwidth decides token speed. When generating text, the GPU reads the model's weights for every token, so speed scales with memory bandwidth. The 5090's bandwidth advantage of about 78% translates to faster generation for models that fit on both cards.
  • Compute matters for prompts, images and training. Prompt processing (prefill), image generation and fine-tuning are more compute-bound, where the 5090's extra cores and newer tensor cores help.

Local LLMs: what each card can run

Approximate fit for single-user use with an 8K context (weights + KV cache + overhead):

Upper-bound token speed for an 8B model at Q4 (~4.8 GB): about 210 tokens/s on the 4090 versus about 370 tokens/s on the 5090, based on bandwidth; real speeds are typically 50–80% of these bounds. Use our VRAM guide and best GPU for local LLMs for other models.

Stable Diffusion, FLUX and video

See best GPU for Stable Diffusion and What is a diffusion model?.

Fine-tuning and training

With QLoRA, both cards can fine-tune 7B–14B models. The 5090's extra 8 GB allows longer sequences, larger batches or bigger models (around 20–32B with careful settings). Neither consumer card supports NVLink, so multi-GPU training relies on PCIe. For serious training, renting data center GPUs is often more practical. See What is fine-tuning?.

FP4: the 5090's new trick

Fifth-generation tensor cores support FP4, which halves memory and roughly doubles tensor throughput compared with FP8 for models and runtimes that support it. Adoption in consumer tools is growing but not universal; most local LLM users still run GGUF quantizations that do not depend on FP4 hardware. See NVFP4 explained and how tensor cores actually work.

Power, heat and practical concerns

  • Power: the 5090 draws up to 575 W; NVIDIA recommends a 1,000 W power supply. The 4090 recommends 850 W.
  • Connector: both use the 16-pin 12VHPWR/12V-2x6 connector; seat it fully and avoid sharp cable bends.
  • Size and cooling: both are large cards; check case clearance and airflow.
  • Availability: street prices for the 5090 have often been well above its launch price, and the 4090 is discontinued, so used prices vary. See why GPU prices are rising.

Value comparison

Cloud rates for consumer GPUs are low on marketplaces. According to our GPU cloud price tracker, RTX 5090 rentals have been listed from about $0.29 per hour and RTX 4090s from about $0.26 per hour, with typical prices higher. If you need a GPU only occasionally, renting can be cheaper; see rent vs buy a GPU.

Which should you buy?

  • Buy the RTX 5090 if you want 32B models at high quality, full-precision FLUX, video generation, faster fine-tuning, or the longest useful life.
  • Buy a used RTX 4090 if 24 GB covers your models and you want strong performance for less.
  • Consider a used RTX 3090 if budget is tight and VRAM matters more than speed.
  • Consider a Mac or DGX Spark if you need to run 70B+ models on one machine and can accept slower generation. See NVIDIA DGX Spark explained.

For a deeper look at the newer card alone, read is the RTX 5090 good for AI?.

Frequently asked questions

How much faster is the RTX 5090 than the 4090 for AI?

It depends on the workload. For memory-bound LLM token generation, the theoretical advantage is around 1.7× from bandwidth; for compute-heavy tasks like image generation, gains are often smaller but still significant. FP4-optimised workloads can see larger jumps.

Is 24 GB enough for local AI?

For most 7B–14B models, SDXL and quantized FLUX, yes. For 32B models at higher quality, unquantized FLUX and large video models, 32 GB is noticeably better.

Can I run two RTX 5090s together?

Yes, across PCIe, using model splitting in tools like llama.cpp or vLLM. There is no NVLink bridge, so communication is slower than on data center GPUs.

Is the RTX 5090 good for training large models?

It is good for fine-tuning and training small to mid-sized models. Training large models needs data center GPUs with more memory and fast interconnects.

content:
Short answer

Every major chipmaker now builds dedicated matrix multiplication units for AI, under different names. NVIDIA Tensor Cores (in GeForce, RTX PRO and data center GPUs) are the most widely used, backed by CUDA. AMD Matrix Cores power Instinct accelerators such as the MI300X and MI355X, while Radeon GPUs use WMMA-based AI accelerators. Intel XMX engines sit in Arc GPUs, and Gaudi accelerators use Matrix Multiplication Engines. Apple's Neural Engine handles on-device AI, with M5-generation chips adding neural accelerators inside the GPU. Google's TPUs are built around giant systolic-array MXUs. The hardware ideas are similar; the biggest differences are in precision support, scale and, above all, software.

The common idea

All these units accelerate the same operation: matrix multiply-accumulate (D = A × B + C) on small tiles, with low-precision inputs and higher-precision accumulation. They reuse each loaded value many times, which is far more efficient than general-purpose cores. For the mechanics, see how tensor cores actually work and What is a tensor core?.

At a glance

NVIDIA Tensor Cores

Introduced with Volta in 2017, now in their fifth generation with Blackwell. Strengths: the broadest precision support (down to FP4 with block scaling, see NVFP4), structured sparsity, mature libraries and support in every major AI framework. Present in consumer cards (RTX 30/40/50), workstation cards and data center GPUs, so the same code runs from a laptop to a supercomputer. See tensor core generations.

AMD Matrix Cores (CDNA)

AMD's Instinct accelerators include Matrix Cores that execute MFMA (matrix fused multiply-add) instructions. The MI300X pairs them with 192 GB of HBM3, and later parts raise memory and add lower precisions; the MI355X supports FP6 and FP4. AMD's advantage has often been memory capacity, which helps run large models on fewer GPUs. The main challenge has been software maturity: ROCm has improved a lot, and major frameworks and inference engines support it, but CUDA's ecosystem remains broader. See AMD vs NVIDIA for AI and MI355X vs B200.

AMD WMMA on Radeon (RDNA)

Consumer Radeon GPUs since RDNA 3 include AI accelerators that execute WMMA (wave matrix multiply-accumulate) instructions. RDNA 4 roughly doubled AI throughput and added FP8 and sparsity support. They are less powerful than CDNA Matrix Cores or NVIDIA's data center tensor cores, but useful for local AI and FSR upscaling.

Intel XMX and Gaudi

Intel's Xe Matrix Extensions (XMX) are systolic matrix engines inside Arc graphics cards and data center GPUs, used for XeSS upscaling and AI inference through OpenVINO and oneAPI. Intel's Gaudi accelerators are separate chips with large Matrix Multiplication Engines and integrated Ethernet networking, positioned as cost-effective training and inference alternatives.

Apple Neural Engine and GPU neural accelerators

Apple's Neural Engine is a power-efficient NPU in iPhones, iPads and Macs, used for features such as Face ID, photo processing and Apple Intelligence through Core ML. Its specifications are not documented in the same detail as GPUs. With the M5 generation, Apple added neural accelerators inside each GPU core, boosting AI performance for apps using Metal and frameworks like MLX. Macs also benefit from large unified memory, letting big models fit even though peak compute is lower than high-end NVIDIA GPUs. See What is an AI PC?.

Google TPU MXUs

Google's Tensor Processing Units are built around Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs): large systolic arrays in which data flows rhythmically through a grid of multiply-accumulate cells, so each value is reused many times with minimal memory traffic. Earlier TPUs used 128 × 128 MXUs; Trillium (TPU v6e) moved to 256 × 256. TPUs are available through Google Cloud and power Google's own Gemini models. See TPU vs GPU, Google Ironwood and NPU vs GPU vs TPU.

Design approaches compared

See What is an AI accelerator? for the full landscape.

Why software matters more than the hardware name

All these units can multiply matrices quickly. What decides real-world results:

  • Framework support: does PyTorch, JAX or your inference engine run well on it?
  • Libraries and kernels: are attention, quantized formats and new model architectures optimised?
  • Precision formats: can it run FP8 or FP4 efficiently for your model?
  • Ecosystem: tutorials, community, cloud availability and debugging tools.

NVIDIA's lead comes largely from CUDA's two-decade head start; see What is CUDA?. AMD and others narrow the gap with open software and strong memory specs.

Which should you choose?

Compare cloud rental prices across GPU types in our GPU cloud price tracker.

Frequently asked questions

Do AMD GPUs have tensor cores?

Not under that name. AMD Instinct accelerators have Matrix Cores, and Radeon GPUs have WMMA-based AI accelerators that do a similar job.

Is Apple's Neural Engine a tensor core?

It is a separate neural processing unit rather than part of the GPU. From the M5 generation, Apple's GPU cores also include neural accelerators, which are closer in concept to tensor cores.

Are TPUs faster than tensor cores?

For large, matrix-heavy workloads in Google Cloud, TPUs are very efficient. NVIDIA GPUs are more flexible and widely supported. Performance depends on the specific chips, precision and software.

Can PyTorch use AMD Matrix Cores?

Yes, through the ROCm build of PyTorch on supported AMD GPUs.
